issues.location: "How do you update a file so a crash can never leave it half-written?" section, sentence beginning "File.Replace offers a close variant of this same pattern..."
issues.problem: Fabricated direct quotation. The article attributes the exact words 'must be on the same drive' to File.Replace Method's own documentation, in quotation marks, with a citation. I fetched the live page (learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.io.file.replace) in full, including both overloads' Remarks sections and every Exception entry, and that phrase does not appear anywhere on the page. The actual, closest statement is: 'If the sourceFileName and destinationFileName are on different volumes, this method raises an exception. If the destinationBackupFileName is on a different volume from the source file, the backup file will be deleted.' That is a different claim in different words (an exception-on-mismatch condition, not a stated 'must be on the same drive' requirement, and it also covers the backup file's volume, which the invented quote omits). The underlying gist -- same-volume is required for the main replace -- happens to be roughly right, but presenting invented wording as a verbatim quote from a real, linked source is exactly the fabrication the brief's rules forbid.
issues.fixLooksLike: Drop the quotation marks and paraphrase: 'though its documentation is explicit that a mismatched volume between source and destination raises an exception' (File.Replace Method), or quote an actual sentence from the page verbatim if a quote is wanted at all.

issues.location: "What breaks if the system crashes mid-update, and how does a journal fix it?" section, sentence beginning "ext4's documentation states the purpose directly..."
issues.problem: Altered quotation via a bracketed word substitution that changes the source's actual wording. The article renders: 'should the system crash during the second [real] write, the journal can be replayed all the way to the latest commit record, guaranteeing the atomicity of whatever gets written through the journal to the disk.' I fetched the live page (docs.kernel.org/filesystems/ext4/journal.html) and the actual sentence reads: 'Should the system crash during the second slow write, the journal can be replayed all the way to the latest commit record, guaranteeing the atomicity of whatever gets written through the journal to the disk.' The source's own word is 'slow', not 'real' -- the bracket is being used to swap the author's chosen word for a different one, not to add neutral clarifying context to an otherwise-verbatim quote. That is quote alteration, even though the rest of the sentence and the underlying claim (replay-to-commit-record atomicity) are accurately rendered.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either quote the source's actual word -- 'during the second slow write' -- or drop the quotation marks around that clause and describe it in the article's own words (e.g. 'during the second, real-location write').

issues.location: Same section, sentence beginning "File.Move's own documentation draws the matching line for .NET: a same-volume move is a single filesystem operation..."
issues.problem: Overstates what the cited source actually says. I fetched File.Move's live documentation in full; it states that a cross-volume move 'is equivalent to copying the file and deleting it from the source' (accurately quoted in the article) but never states, anywhere, that a same-volume move is a single filesystem operation or is atomic -- the article's framing ('the matching line for .NET') presents an inference by exclusion as if the documentation asserted it directly. The underlying claim is very likely true of the .NET implementation (a same-volume File.Move ultimately calls the OS rename primitive), but the article doesn't cite anything that actually says so -- unlike the adjacent WriteToFile claim, where the writer did go to the dotnet/runtime source to substantiate a similar implementation-level claim.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either soften to something like 'implies, by leaving only the cross-volume case as copy-and-delete, that a same-volume move is something cheaper' without presenting it as documentation's own words, or pull the same-volume behavior from the dotnet/runtime File.Move source the way the article already does for WriteToFile.
